title: Probability Spaces Random Variables and Expectation

items.title: Basic identities for a probability measure
items.strategy: Specialize the published measure monotonicity, difference, subadditivity, inclusion-exclusion, and continuity theorems to a measure of total mass 1, so complements and the union bound become probability identities without rebuilding the measure theory.

items.title: Finite probability spaces are exactly finite full-power-set probability spaces
items.strategy: In the full-power-set case the atoms are singletons, so a probability measure is determined by its singleton masses; conversely the published finite weight data already gives the power-set probability formula, including zero-weight outcomes.

items.title: Agreement with the published finite probability-space definition
Random elements and real random variables
Finite random variables are measurable
items.strategy: On a finite full-power-set probability space every preimage of a Borel set is just a subset of the sample space, hence an event; this identifies the published finite random-variable definition with the measurable-map definition.

items.title: Law or distribution of a random element
The law of a random element is a probability measure
items.strategy: Preimages under a measurable map preserve the empty set, the whole space, and countable disjoint unions, so the pushforward set function is countably additive and has total mass 1.

items.title: Laws commute with measurable maps
items.strategy: For a measurable outer map g, compare both laws on each measurable target set B by the identity (g o X)^(-1)(B) = X^(-1)(g^(-1)(B)).

items.title: Cumulative distribution function of a real random variable
Probability laws correspond to distribution functions
items.strategy: View the law of a real random variable as a Borel probability measure on R, apply the published Lebesgue-Stieltjes correspondence, and translate its interval formula into the probability notation F_X(x) = P(X <= x).

items.title: Atoms and continuity points of a law
Expectation of a nonnegative or integrable random variable
Expectation depends only on the almost-everywhere class
items.strategy: Reduce both nonnegative and integrable cases to the published almost-everywhere invariance of the Lebesgue integral, so expectation descends to the L^1-class.

items.title: Change of variables for expectation
items.strategy: First check that g o X is measurable, then identify the two sides on indicators and extend through the pushforward-law definition so the formula is proved at the level of the actual measure, not only for simple special cases.

items.title: Expectation agrees with the published finite weighted sum
items.strategy: Combine the finite full-power-set identification with change of variables, then compare the resulting integral with the published finite expectation and expectation-by-distribution formulas.

items.title: The expectation of an indicator is the probability of the event
items.strategy: Treat the indicator as a nonnegative random variable and integrate the two-valued function directly, so its expectation is exactly the measure of the event.

items.title: Layer-cake formulas for random variables
items.strategy: Apply the published layer-cake theorem at exponent p = 1 to X^+ and X^-, then recombine the two tails by the positive-negative decomposition.

items.title: Linearity, monotonicity, and the modulus bound for expectation
items.strategy: Specialize the linearity, monotonicity, and triangle inequality of the Lebesgue integral to probability notation.

items.title: Moments, variance, and covariance on a probability space
Variance and covariance identities for random variables
items.strategy: Expand the centered square and centered product inside expectation, then collect the terms by linearity exactly as in the finite case but without finite-support assumptions.

items.title: Jensen's inequality for expectation
items.strategy: Apply the published Jensen inequality for probability measures to the expectation integral, keeping the finite-convex-function hypotheses visible.

items.title: Markov's inequality for random variables
items.strategy: Read the event {X >= a} as the superlevel set in the published integral Markov inequality and specialize from a general measure to probability.

items.title: Chebyshev's inequality for random variables
items.strategy: Apply Markov to the nonnegative square (X - E[X])^2 and rewrite its expectation as the variance.

items.title: Holder's inequality for random variables
items.strategy: Apply the published Holder inequality in the probability-measure case, with the endpoint conventions inherited unchanged.

items.title: Cauchy-Schwarz for random variables
items.strategy: Either specialize the previous Holder corollary at p = q = 2 or cite the published L^2 corollary directly; both give the same probability-space inequality and equality convention.

items.title: Lyapunov's moment inequality on a probability space
items.strategy: Specialize the finite-measure L^r-to-L^p inclusion theorem to a measure of total mass 1, so the prefactor collapses to 1.

items.title: The second-moment lower bound for positive probability
items.strategy: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to X 1_{X > 0} and 1_{X > 0}, then rewrite the second factor as the probability of {X > 0}.

items.title: The general inequalities restrict to the published finite ones
Normal equations for best affine $L^2$ prediction
items.strategy: Work in the L^2(P) quotient so equality is almost sure, identify the affine predictors with the finite-dimensional subspace span{1, Y_1, ..., Y_n}, expand the squared error into a quadratic form in the coefficients, and characterize minimizers by the covariance normal equations; the predictor is unique as an L^2 class even when the coefficient vector is not.

items.title: Best affine prediction from one random variable
items.strategy: Solve the one-equation normal system explicitly when Var(Y) > 0, and treat the zero-variance case separately so coefficient nonuniqueness is not mistaken for predictor nonuniqueness.

title: Probability Spaces Random Variables and Expectation — Examples

items.title: A countable probability space with geometric weights
items.strategy: Normalize the geometric weights on N, treat the coordinate map as a random variable, then compute its law and expectation directly from the series.

items.title: The uniform random variable on [0,1]
items.strategy: Use Lebesgue measure on [0,1], compute the distribution function directly, and recover moments and tails by integration.

items.title: Recovering an exponential law from its tail
items.strategy: Start from P(X > t) = exp(-lambda t), recover the distribution function and law, and then compute the expectation from the tail integral.

items.title: Discrete, continuous, and mixed distribution functions
items.strategy: Compare a step law, an absolutely continuous law, and a mixed law to show how jumps and continuity points encode atoms without implying the existence of a density.

items.title: Expectation under a measurable transformation
items.strategy: Compute a nonlinear expectation by pushing the variable to its law and integrating on the target rather than on the original sample space.

items.title: Jensen for logarithm and exponential
items.strategy: Apply Jensen to the concave logarithm and the convex exponential under their exact integrability and positivity hypotheses, yielding the weighted AM-GM and exponential-moment inequalities.

items.title: Markov and Chebyshev sharpness
items.strategy: Exhibit simple two-point laws attaining equality and contrast them with broader distributions where the bounds are weak, so sharpness is not confused with concentration.

items.title: A random variable need not have a finite expectation
items.strategy: Use a heavy-tailed positive law with divergent harmonic-type first moment, so the expectation exists only as +infinity rather than as a finite number.

items.title: A distribution function need not have a density
items.strategy: Take a Bernoulli law: its distribution function has jumps at the atoms, so no Lebesgue density can reproduce those point masses.

items.title: Equality almost surely is not pointwise equality
items.strategy: Modify a variable on a nonempty null set inside a continuous probability space; the two representatives agree almost surely and have the same expectation, but they are not pointwise equal.

items.title: Bertrand's chord paradox is a model-specification problem
items.strategy: Compare three explicit random-chord models on the same geometric question to show that the answer changes with the sample space and law, not with the geometry alone.
